bayway.summary: Between merchants an additional term in a confirmation becomes part of the contract unless the party opposing it proves material alteration, meaning surprise (subjective and objective, the latter shown by trade usage) or hardship; a customary clause shifting excise taxes to the buyer was neither surprising to a reasonable merchant nor a hardship the buyer could not have avoided.

sections.Parties: Bayway Refining Company, a refiner that sold a gasoline blending component, was the plaintiff and appellee; its parent, Tosco Corporation, joined on a separate claim it lost and did not appeal. Oxygenated Marketing and Trading A.G. (OMT), the buyer, was the defendant, counterclaimant and appellant. Bayway sought reimbursement of $464,035.12 in federal excise tax under a tax-allocation clause in its confirmation; OMT said the clause never entered the contract because it materially altered the bargain. Both were merchants in petroleum products.
sections.Material Facts: In February 1998 the parties agreed by telephone that Bayway would sell OMT 60,000 barrels of MTBE, a gasoline blendstock. On February 12 OMT faxed a confirmation reciting the deal and calling itself the entire contract. On February 13 Bayway faxed its own confirmation incorporating by reference “Bayway Refining Company’s General Terms and Conditions dated March 01, 1994”; paragraph 10, the Tax Clause, made the buyer pay any federal, state or local excise and similar taxes, other than income taxes, that the seller incurred on the product sold. OMT did not object and took delivery on March 22. Under 26 U.S.C. § 4081 a sale of taxable fuel to a buyer not registered with the IRS is a taxable event; OMT was unregistered, so the sale generated $464,035.12 in excise tax, which Bayway paid and demanded back. OMT refused. There was no prior course of dealing allocating taxes differently.
sections.Procedural History: Bayway and Tosco sued OMT in the Southern District of New York under diversity jurisdiction. On Bayway’s summary-judgment motion Judge McKenna held the Tax Clause incorporated under UCC § 2-207(2) and entered judgment for Bayway. OMT had first raised material alteration in its opposition papers; Bayway answered with reply affidavits on petroleum-industry custom, and OMT neither sought leave for a sur-reply nor claimed contrary evidence. On appeal OMT argued material alteration and improper consideration of the reply evidence, and for the first time that Bayway’s real acceptance was a broker’s confirmation and that OMT’s integration clause was an objection under § 2-207(2)(c); the Second Circuit (Jacobs, J., with Winter, C.J., and Calabresi, J.) reviewed de novo, declined to reach the new arguments, and affirmed on June 8, 2000.
sections.Issue: When a merchant’s confirmation adds a term to a contract already made orally and the other merchant says the term materially alters the contract under § 2-207(2)(b), who bears the burden of proving material alteration? Did OMT carry it as to the Tax Clause, and could the district court consider industry-custom evidence first offered in reply?
sections.Holding: Between merchants an additional term in a definite acceptance or written confirmation becomes part of the contract unless one of § 2-207(2)’s three exceptions applies; because the statute presumes inclusion, the party opposing the term bears the burden of proving material alteration. A term materially alters the contract if its incorporation without the other party’s express awareness would result in surprise or hardship. Surprise has a subjective element (what the objecting party knew) and an objective element (what a reasonable merchant should have known). OMT showed only subjective surprise, unrebutted evidence showed that industry custom puts excise taxes on the buyer, and any hardship was limited, routine and self-inflicted because registering with the IRS would have avoided the tax.
sections.Reasoning: The burden question was one of first impression in the circuit. Because subsection (2) says additional terms “become part of the contract unless” an exception applies, inclusion is the default and the party invoking an exception must prove it, as the Tenth, First and Seventh Circuits had held in Avedon, JOM and Comark. OMT’s executives called the clause a “contract by ambush,” which showed subjective surprise, but objective surprise required proof that a reasonable merchant would not have expected the term, and the record ran the other way: two unchallenged industry experts said buyers customarily pay all taxes on a petroleum sale, and of the five competitors’ forms OMT produced, three mirrored the clause, Chevron’s folded taxes into price and Texaco’s was silent. On hardship, the cry rang hollow: the clause imposed a routine, transaction-specific obligation OMT could have avoided by registering,. Whether hardship alone can ever establish material alteration was left undecided.

northrop.summary: When an acceptance’s term conflicts with the offer’s, Illinois would follow the majority “knockout” rule: both terms drop out and the Code’s gap-filler governs, so the seller’s 90-day warranty and the buyer’s unlimited warranty were replaced by § 2-309’s reasonable time, which six months of complex testing satisfied.

sections.Parties: Northrop Corporation, a large defense contractor that builds weapons systems using electronic components, was the buyer, the plaintiff below, and the appellee and cross-appellant. Litronic Industries, a much smaller maker of printed wire boards, was the seller, the defendant, and the appellant. Northrop sought back what it had paid for boards that failed inspection; Litronic said its 90-day warranty governed and had expired before Northrop rejected the boards. Both were merchants, and Illinois law governed the diversity action.
sections.Material Facts: In 1987 Northrop solicited bids for four customized “1714” printed wire boards for a defense system. Litronic mailed an offer to sell four boards at $19,000 each with delivery in six weeks; the offer stated a 90-day warranty in lieu of all others. Northrop’s purchasing officer, Lynch, telephoned Litronic’s representative, Lair, promised a formal purchase order for all four boards, and said enough to make clear that Northrop’s acceptance carried different terms. A “turn on” letter authorizing production followed a month later, and the purchase order, which called for a written acknowledgment and contained a warranty with no time limit, arrived months after that. The first three boards were delivered in July 1988. After five or six months of testing Northrop concluded in December 1988 and January 1989 that they were defective and tried to return them; Litronic refused because its 90-day warranty had lapsed.
sections.Procedural History: Northrop sued in federal court in Illinois under diversity jurisdiction and the case was tried to a magistrate judge, who held that the conflicting warranty terms cancelled each other under § 2-207, that § 2-309 supplied a reasonable time, that six months was reasonable given the complexity of the testing, and entered judgment for Northrop for $58,000, the price of the three delivered boards. He disbelieved Northrop’s claim to have returned other defective boards and denied recovery for boards neither returned nor accounted for. Litronic appealed; Northrop cross-appealed, invoking § 2-711(3). The Seventh Circuit (Posner, C.J., with Ripple, J., and Hill, J., of the Eleventh Circuit sitting by designation) reviewed the facts for clear error, had to predict unsettled Illinois law, and affirmed on July 18, 1994; Judge Ripple concurred separately.
sections.Issue: Section 2-207(1) makes a response an acceptance though it states terms “additional to or different from” the offer, but § 2-207(2) says what happens only to “additional” terms. When the acceptance’s term conflicts with the offer’s, does the offeror’s term control, does the different term drop out under the materiality analysis, or do both fall away in favor of the Code’s gap-fillers? Which rule would Illinois adopt, and was Northrop’s rejection five or six months after delivery timely under it? May a buyer keep rejected goods as security under § 2-711(3) without accounting for them?
sections.Holding: Illinois would follow the majority rule, commonly called the knockout rule though the opinion does not use the phrase: conflicting terms in offer and acceptance cancel each other and the Code’s gap-fillers supply the missing term. Litronic’s 90-day warranty and Northrop’s unlimited warranty were materially different, so both dropped out and § 2-309’s reasonable-time standard governed; the finding that six months was reasonable for these custom boards was not clearly erroneous, so the rejection was timely. A buyer that rightfully rejects goods holds a security interest under § 2-711(3) and may hold or resell them, but one that neither returns the goods nor explains what became of them cannot recover their price, because the omission leaves open an inference of double recovery. Affirmed in full.
sections.Reasoning: Three views have developed. California in Steiner v. Mobil Oil treats different terms like additional terms and asks only whether they materially alter the contract, which Posner called possibly the most sensible approach. The leading minority view, applied by the Fourth Circuit in Valtrol, ignores the discrepant terms in the acceptance so the offeror’s terms control. The majority view, applied by the Tenth Circuit in Daitom, knocks out both terms and inserts a gap-filler. Declaring none of them correct, the court reasoned as a predictor: Illinois courts tend to adopt majority UCC rules and the Code prizes uniformity, so Illinois would follow the majority. Lynch had not made the broader warranty a condition of acceptance, so the expressly-conditional proviso was not in play; both warranties vanished and § 2-309 filled the gap, giving Northrop a warranty of reasonable duration “courtesy the court.”

northrop.separateOpinions: Judge Ripple concurred in the judgment and in the prediction of Illinois law but declined to express a view on which reading of § 2-207 is best; that policy choice belongs to the state courts and to the Uniform Law Commissioners, whose drafting committee was then revising Article 2, and federal judges should offer their views there rather than in opinions predicting state law.

hill-gateway.summary: A vendor, as master of the offer, may invite acceptance by conduct, so a buyer who receives a computer with terms stating that keeping it beyond 30 days is acceptance, and keeps it, is bound by those terms including arbitration; § 2-207 does not apply to a one-form transaction, and the Federal Arbitration Act forbids demanding special prominence for an arbitration clause.

sections.Parties: Rich and Enza Hill, who bought a Gateway computer by telephone, were the plaintiffs and appellees, suing on behalf of a class of purchasers and wanting their claims heard in court. Gateway 2000, Inc., a direct seller of personal computers by telephone and mail order, and David Prais, an individual defendant whose role the opinion does not describe, were the defendants and appellants seeking to enforce the arbitration clause shipped with the computer.
sections.Material Facts: The Hills ordered a Gateway computer by telephone and gave a credit-card number. The box arrived with the computer, software and a four-page statement of terms that by its own words governed unless the customer returned the computer within 30 days; one term was an arbitration clause. Gateway’s advertisements said its products came with limited warranties and lifetime support. The Hills kept the computer more than 30 days before complaining about its components and performance. They conceded noticing the statement of terms but denied reading it closely enough to find the agreement to arbitrate, and the box carried no notice on its exterior that terms were inside.
sections.Procedural History: The Hills sued in federal court in Illinois, alleging that the computer’s shortcomings made Gateway a racketeer under RICO, with mail and wire fraud as the predicate offenses, and seeking treble damages for themselves and a class. Gateway moved to enforce the arbitration clause under the Federal Arbitration Act; the district court refused, finding the record insufficient to show a valid arbitration agreement or adequate notice of the clause. Gateway took an interlocutory appeal under 9 U.S.C. § 16(a)(1)(A). The Seventh Circuit (Easterbrook, J., with Cummings and Wood, JJ.) vacated and remanded with instructions to compel arbitration on January 6, 1997; rehearing was denied and the Supreme Court denied certiorari, 522 U.S. 808.
sections.Issue: Did the Hills accept Gateway’s terms, including the arbitration clause, by keeping the computer beyond the 30-day return period, so that the Federal Arbitration Act requires enforcement? Does ProCD v. Zeidenberg extend beyond software and beyond contracts still to be performed on both sides? Does § 2-207 govern a transaction with only one form? Does the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act or any requirement that an arbitration clause be conspicuous defeat the clause?
sections.Holding: Yes, and the clause is enforceable. A vendor, as master of the offer, may invite acceptance by conduct and may propose limits on the kind of conduct that constitutes acceptance; a buyer who receives goods with terms, can read them and return the goods, and instead keeps them past the stated period accepts the terms, whether or not the buyer read them. That rule is about contract formation generally, not software, and applies where the buyer pays before seeing the full terms. Section 2-207 has no application when there is only one form. Magnuson-Moss does not require a seller to recite its terms before the sale, and the FAA forbids any special requirement that an arbitration clause be prominent. By keeping the computer beyond 30 days the Hills accepted Gateway’s offer, arbitration clause included.
sections.Reasoning: ProCD controlled: a vendor may propose that a contract be formed only after the customer inspects both product and terms, with retention as acceptance and return as rejection. A contract need not be read to be effective. If a sales representative had to read four pages of terms before taking a credit-card number, “the droning voice would anesthetize rather than enlighten many potential buyers.” The Hills’ distinctions failed: “ProCD is about the law of contract, not the law of software”; the executory-contract objection confused formation with performance, and both contracts were in any event incompletely performed because Gateway owed warranty and lifetime support; shoppers can learn terms by asking (Magnuson-Moss requires warranty terms on request), from public sources, or by inspecting on delivery and returning, and the Hills chose the third route. Section 2-207 addresses conflicting forms exchanged by two parties, so it was irrelevant to one form. Under Doctor’s Associates v. Casarotto the FAA bars singling out arbitration clauses for special notice, so the terms stand or fall together.

klocek.summary: In a consumer purchase the buyer is ordinarily the offeror and the vendor accepts by shipping, so terms in the box are additional terms under § 2-207 even though only one form exists; because the buyer was not a merchant they became part of the contract only on his express assent, which keeping the computer five days did not show, and Gateway failed to prove an agreement to arbitrate.

sections.Parties: William S. Klocek, a consumer representing himself, was the plaintiff. Gateway, Inc., which sold him a computer, and Hewlett-Packard, Inc., which made a scanner he bought to use with it, were the defendants. Gateway sought dismissal and an order compelling arbitration under paragraph 10 of its Standard Terms and Conditions Agreement; Hewlett-Packard moved to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. Klocek sought damages, individually and for a class, for products that did not work as promised and false promises of technical support.
sections.Material Facts: Klocek’s complaint said he lived in Missouri; Gateway’s affidavit said only that it shipped a computer to him on or about August 31, 1997, while Klocek said he bought it in person at Gateway’s store in Overland Park, Kansas, on August 27 and took it with him. The box contained the computer, a battery, cables, manuals and Gateway’s Standard Terms and Conditions Agreement, four pages with sixteen paragraphs. A boxed notice at the top of the first page said that by keeping the computer beyond five days after delivery the customer accepted the terms. Paragraph 10 required arbitration of any dispute under the rules of the International Chamber of Commerce in Chicago before a sole arbitrator. Gateway offered no evidence that at the sale it told Klocek about the terms, the five-day period or the arbitration clause; its evidence showed only that it enclosed the document to be read afterwards.
sections.Procedural History: Klocek sued in the District of Kansas under diversity jurisdiction. On November 22, 1999 Gateway moved to dismiss and compel arbitration under 9 U.S.C. §§ 3–4; Hewlett-Packard moved to dismiss because the damages alleged against it fell short of the $75,000 amount in controversy. Judge Kathryn H. Vratil applied a summary-judgment-like standard: Gateway bore the initial burden of showing an enforceable agreement to arbitrate before the burden shifted to Klocek. On June 15, 2000 she overruled Gateway’s motion, sustained Hewlett-Packard’s, and gave Gateway until June 30 to file a supplemental motion if it contended some other state’s law applied, reserving a possible jury trial on whether an arbitration agreement existed. The action was later dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction and the ruling was never reviewed on appeal.
sections.Issue: Did Klocek agree to the arbitration clause in the Standard Terms? That required deciding whether to follow Hill and ProCD; whether § 2-207 applies when only one party’s form exists; which party was the offeror; whether Gateway’s acceptance was expressly conditional on assent to the terms; and whether a nonmerchant buyer expressly assents to additional terms by keeping the goods beyond a stated period.
sections.Holding: In a typical consumer transaction the purchaser is the offeror and the vendor accepts by completing the sale or shipping the goods, so terms shipped with the goods are additional terms in an acceptance or written confirmation, and § 2-207 applies although only one form exists. Where the buyer is not a merchant, additional terms are proposals that enter the contract only if the buyer expressly agrees, and express assent cannot be presumed from silence or failure to object. Gateway offered no evidence that it was the offeror, that it conditioned the sale on the terms, or that Klocek expressly agreed; keeping the computer beyond five days did not show express agreement on this record, so Gateway failed to prove an agreement to arbitrate.
sections.Reasoning: Judge Vratil declined to follow Hill and ProCD: the Seventh Circuit had concluded without support that § 2-207 is irrelevant when only one form is involved. By its terms § 2-207 applies to “an acceptance or written confirmation” and requires no second form, and Official Comment 1 says it covers an agreement reached orally and followed by one party’s memorandum adding terms. In typical consumer transactions the purchaser is the offeror and the vendor the offeree; a vendor can be the offeror in a particular deal, so the court assumed Klocek offered to buy and Gateway accepted by completing the sale or shipping. Gateway’s acceptance was not expressly conditional, because a conditional acceptance must clearly express unwillingness to proceed without the added terms and shipping goods with terms inside communicated nothing of the kind at the time of sale. Because Klocek was not a merchant, the terms were proposals requiring his express agreement; Gateway’s own declaration that retention would count as assent, with no evidence that the five-day period was discussed or made a condition of sale, did not prove it.

mattei.summary: A buyer’s promise made “subject to” obtaining leases satisfactory to him is not illusory, because where satisfaction turns on judgment rather than measurable commercial quality the buyer must exercise that judgment honestly and in good faith, and that duty is consideration enough for the seller’s promise to convey.

sections.Parties: Peter O. Mattei, a real-estate developer assembling land for a shopping center, was the plaintiff and appellant; he signed the buyer’s side of the deposit receipt, paid the deposit, pursued leases and sought damages when the conveyance failed. Amelia F. Hopper, owner of the adjacent parcel, was the defendant and respondent; she offered to sell, later repudiated through counsel, and won at trial. Coldwell Banker & Company was the real-estate intermediary charged with obtaining leases satisfactory to Mattei.
sections.Material Facts: Mattei planned a shopping center on land beside Hopper’s parcel. After an agent had negotiated with her for months and she had rejected several proposals as too low, Hopper submitted an offer that Mattei accepted the same day on the agent’s deposit-receipt form. The price was $57,500; Mattei deposited $1,000 with the agent and had 120 days to examine title and close, the balance falling due when Hopper tendered a good and sufficient deed. The final clause made the transaction “subject to Coldwell Banker & Company obtaining leases satisfactory to the purchaser,” so that Mattei could line up tenants before paying the balance. Mattei paid the deposit and pursued leases. Before the 120 days ran, Hopper’s attorney told him she would not sell on the deposit receipt’s terms. Hopper later received notice that satisfactory leases had been obtained and that Mattei offered the balance, and she withheld the deed.
sections.Procedural History: Mattei sued for damages for breach of the written land-sale agreement. After a bench trial the court held that the satisfaction clause left performance within Mattei’s unrestricted choice, that the agreement was therefore illusory and lacking in mutuality, and entered judgment for Hopper. The Supreme Court of California, sitting in bank, reversed on October 24, 1958; Justice Spence wrote, joined by Chief Justice Gibson and Justices Shenk, Carter, Traynor and Schauer, and Justice McComb dissented without opinion. The decision resolved enforceability and did not fix a damages amount.
sections.Issue: Did the signed deposit receipt create an immediate contract whose performance was conditioned on Mattei’s obtaining satisfactory leases? And did the satisfaction clause impose a legally enforceable standard on Mattei’s judgment, so that his promise supplied consideration for Hopper’s promise to convey?
sections.Holding: Yes to both. The deposit receipt became a binding contract when signed; the lease clause made Mattei’s duty to complete the purchase conditional on obtaining leases satisfactory to him and gave him a power to terminate if that condition failed. Because Mattei had to evaluate the leases through honest, good-faith judgment, his discretion was legally restricted and his promise was sufficient consideration. The judgment for Hopper was reversed.
sections.Reasoning: The court first read the whole receipt as one present agreement that stated the property, price, deposit, performance period, deed tender and lease condition; the clause allocated leasing risk to Mattei during the 120 days rather than postponing formation until he gave notice that leases had been obtained. In a bilateral contract each promise must impose a legal obligation, and a promise is illusory when its maker keeps unrestricted freedom to perform or withdraw. Satisfaction clauses fall into two classes: where satisfaction concerns commercial value, quality or operative fitness, a reasonable-person standard applies; where it concerns taste, fancy or judgment, the promisor’s honest judgment governs. Shopping-center leases required weighing duration, renewal options, covenants, rent, tenant finances and business mix, calling for business judgment, so Mattei had subjective evaluative authority coupled with a duty to exercise it honestly. Genuine dissatisfaction would excuse him; a fabricated claim of dissatisfaction would be breach, and Hopper could challenge a refusal by proving it lacked genuineness. That exposure was a real legal detriment supporting her promise, even though the leases would come from third parties.

structural-polymer.summary: A requirements contract has consideration as a matter of law even though the buyer began with zero requirements and kept discretion over quality, because UCC § 2-306 binds the buyer to its actual good-faith requirements, the quality term was judged by the buyer’s reasonable opinion, an annual cap bounded expansion, and the seller’s right to match a competing price preserved the buyer’s purchase obligation.

sections.Parties: Structural Polymer Group, Ltd. and Structural Polymer Systems, Ltd., British corporations referred to together as SP, made prepreg from carbon fiber and were the plaintiffs, appellees and cross-appellants. Zoltek Corporation, a Missouri carbon-fiber manufacturer, supplied SP under a 2000 agreement, left the 2005 and 2006 orders unfilled, and was the defendant, appellant and cross-appellee.
sections.Material Facts: In November 2000 the parties signed a Supply Agreement running through December 31, 2010: Zoltek would manufacture and sell all of SP’s requirements for large-tow fiber meeting the Panex 33 specifications at the then-current market price, and SP would buy from Zoltek its total requirements for carbon fiber of suitable quality in SP’s reasonable opinion, up to the prior year’s purchases plus one million pounds. If another supplier offered a lower price Zoltek had a right of first refusal; a match bound SP to buy from Zoltek. SP bought 28,219 pounds in 2000 and 20,944 in 2001, ordered nothing in 2003 after Zoltek replaced Panex 33 with Panex 35 in April 2002, and bought 548,935 pounds of Panex 35 in 2004. The dispute concerned an unfilled 1,480,138-pound order in 2005 and a claimed entitlement to 2,480,138 pounds in 2006. SP also bought small-tow fiber elsewhere.
sections.Procedural History: SP sued Zoltek in the Eastern District of Missouri on February 22, 2005 for breach, seeking lost profits and specific performance and pleading alternative counts for Panex 35 and Panex 33. At trial Judge Carol E. Jackson treated Zoltek’s lack-of-mutuality argument as an unpleaded affirmative defense, denied a late amendment, held that the writing had consideration as a matter of law, and refused an abandonment instruction. On November 29, 2006 the jury awarded $21,138,518 on the Panex 35 count and $14,906,377 on the Panex 33 count and denied future lost profits; because the counts were alternatives for the same maximum quantity, the court vacated the second award under Rule 59(e) and entered judgment for $21,138,518, then denied Zoltek’s Rule 50(b) and 59(a) motions. Zoltek appealed and SP cross-appealed the reduction. The Eighth Circuit (Colloton, J., with Shepherd, J., and Erickson, D.J.) affirmed on October 8, 2008.
sections.Issue: Did SP’s promise to buy its total good-faith requirements of suitable large-tow carbon fiber from Zoltek, subject to an annual cap and Zoltek’s price-matching right, supply consideration even though SP began with zero large-tow requirements and kept judgment about quality? Could SP recover under both alternative product calculations?
sections.Holding: The Supply Agreement had mutuality and consideration as a matter of Missouri law. Section 2-306 as enacted in Missouri imposed good faith on SP’s requirements, the quality phrase used SP’s reasonable opinion, the annual cap constrained expansion, and Zoltek’s right to match a competing price preserved the purchase obligation. The abandonment instruction was properly refused, the lost-profit award was supported, the Gamesa shipment fell outside the offset, and the second alternative award duplicated the first. Affirmed on the appeal and the cross-appeal.
sections.Reasoning: Zoltek’s mutuality argument was really a claim that SP’s side imposed no legal detriment; under Restatement § 79 and Missouri law, once consideration exists mutuality adds nothing, and the sufficiency of consideration in a writing is a question of law. Missouri’s § 400.2-306(1) measures quantity by the buyer’s actual requirements occurring in good faith, so SP promised to order its genuine large-tow needs from Zoltek; zero requirements could result from a good-faith business decision, while a zero chosen to divert covered demand or escape the bargain would support a breach claim. That enforceable standard supplied consideration from the outset, and SP’s later order pattern went to performance, a jury question, not formation. The right of first refusal created a real sequence: SP could present a lower offer, Zoltek could match, a match bound SP to buy from Zoltek, and only an unmatched price freed SP to buy elsewhere. Buying small-tow fiber elsewhere could be breach if SP used an interchangeable product in bad faith to divert covered demand, but the jury found SP’s performance compliant.

wood-lucy.summary: An exclusive agency agreement that gave the agent sole rights to place a designer’s endorsements and market her designs in exchange for half the revenues carried an implied promise to use reasonable efforts, which supplied consideration for her exclusivity promise; “a promise may be lacking, and yet the whole writing may be instinct with an obligation.”

sections.Parties: Otis F. Wood, a marketer with a business organization suited to placing commercial endorsements, was the plaintiff and appellant in the Court of Appeals; the agreement gave him exclusive marketing and licensing authority, and he sued for his share of revenues lost through her independent endorsements. Lucy, Lady Duff-Gordon, a prominent fashion creator whose approval added market value to designs and products, was the defendant and respondent; she granted the exclusive rights, kept approval authority, later made endorsements on her own, and attacked the agreement’s consideration on the pleadings.
sections.Material Facts: The signed agreement, effective April 1, 1915 for at least a year and then year to year unless ended on ninety days’ notice, gave Wood, subject to her approval, the exclusive right to place her endorsement on others’ designs and the exclusive right to sell her own designs or license others to make and sell them. She was to receive one-half of all profits and revenues from contracts Wood made; he was to collect the revenues, remit her share, account monthly, and take out patents, copyrights and trademarks when his judgment found them useful. The writing recited that Wood had a business organization adapted to placing the endorsements she approved but nowhere said in terms that he would use reasonable efforts. Wood alleged full performance and that she had endorsed fabrics, dresses and millinery on her own, excluded him and kept the revenues.
sections.Procedural History: Wood sued for breach, setting out the agreement in full. Lady Duff-Gordon moved under New York code pleading, described in the reports as a demurrer and a motion for judgment on the pleadings, accepting the well-pleaded facts for purposes of testing their legal sufficiency. Special Term denied the motion. The Appellate Division, First Department, unanimously reversed on April 20, 1917, 177 A.D. 624: Justice Davis read the writing as obliging Wood to collect and divide revenues only if he chose to arrange a deal, so his promises supplied neither mutuality nor consideration. The Court of Appeals reversed and affirmed Special Term with costs on December 4, 1917. Judge Cardozo wrote for a four-judge majority (Cuddeback, McLaughlin, Andrews); Chief Judge Hiscock and Judges Chase and Crane dissented without opinion. Performance, breach and damages remained for trial.
sections.Issue: Does a signed exclusive marketing agreement supported by a revenue-sharing structure, monthly accounting and intellectual-property duties, and a recital identifying the marketer’s specialized organization, imply a promise that the marketer will use reasonable efforts, thereby supplying consideration for the fashion creator’s exclusive grant even though the words are absent?
sections.Holding: Yes. Read as a whole in its commercial setting, the writing bound Wood to use reasonable efforts to place Lady Duff-Gordon’s endorsements and market her designs. That implied promise supplied consideration and made her exclusivity promise enforceable, so the complaint stated a contract claim. The Appellate Division was reversed and Special Term’s denial of judgment on the pleadings affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Cardozo drew the obligation from the recitals, grants, compensation formula, duration and express administrative duties operating together in the parties’ planned business. Wood’s acceptance of an exclusive agency for at least a year carried the duty to work the channel he alone controlled; the recital of his business organization identified the intended use for it. Most tellingly, her only compensation was half the revenues his efforts produced, so unless he undertook to make those efforts the transaction could not have had the business efficacy both parties must have intended. The express duties to collect and divide money, account monthly and secure patents, copyrights and trademarks presupposed commercial activity generating contracts and protectable interests, reinforcing the implication that he would bring those predicates into existence. Because an unreasonable failure to develop the business would expose Wood to liability, he had incurred a legal detriment that supported her promise. The Appellate Division had looked for an express sentence compelling Wood to procure deals; Cardozo, asked what commitment the document as a whole conveyed.

dixon.summary: A lender’s promise to consider borrowers for a loan modification if they stopped paying and supplied financial information was too indefinite to be a contract to modify, but definite enough to support promissory estoppel once the borrowers defaulted at its direction and the lender used that default to foreclose; recovery is confined to the value of the reliance.

sections.Parties: Frank and Deana Dixon, homeowners in Scituate, Massachusetts, were the plaintiffs. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., which held the mortgage on their home, was the defendant. The Dixons sought to stop foreclosure and hold Wells Fargo to its promise; Wells Fargo moved to dismiss, arguing that no enforceable promise existed and that federal law preempted the claim.
sections.Material Facts: The facts came from the complaint, taken as true on a motion to dismiss. On or about June 8, 2009 the Dixons and Wells Fargo orally agreed to take the steps needed to enter into a modification of their mortgage loan. Wells Fargo instructed them to stop making payments, told them the unpaid payments would be added to the modified note, and asked for financial information, which they promptly supplied. They stopped paying. Wells Fargo never completed the modification process, and on or about December 8, 2010 the Dixons received notice from the Massachusetts Land Court that Wells Fargo was foreclosing. The home was worth more than the loan balance and arrearage. The Dixons acknowledged that the bank had never promised a modification on particular terms; they sought to hold it to its promise to consider them for one.
sections.Procedural History: The Dixons sued in Massachusetts Superior Court, which enjoined the foreclosure on February 14, 2011. Wells Fargo removed the case to federal court and moved to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6). At a hearing on May 9, 2011 Judge William G. Young dismissed the breach-of-contract claim as insufficiently pleaded and took the promissory-estoppel claim and the preemption defense under advisement. On July 22, 2011, 798 F. Supp. 2d 336, he denied the motion as to promissory estoppel and set the case for the September trial list. The ruling holds only that the allegations stated a claim.
sections.Issue: Does a lender’s promise to consider borrowers for a loan modification if they stop making payments and provide financial information support a promissory-estoppel claim under Massachusetts law, even though the promise is too indefinite to create a contract to modify the loan? Is such a claim preempted by the Home Owners’ Loan Act and its regulations?
sections.Holding: Yes, and no. Massachusetts enforces promises by virtue of reliance under Restatement (Second) § 90. The promise must be definite enough to show a commitment but need not be comprehensive enough to be an offer that could ripen into a contract. A promise to consider borrowers for a modification, conditioned on their defaulting and supplying financial information, was sufficiently definite when they took those steps in reasonable reliance and the lender then used the default to foreclose. Recovery is confined to the value of the reliance, which avoids converting negotiations into a binding modification. The claim was not preempted because it enforces a general duty to honor promises that binds all businesses rather than regulating lending.
sections.Reasoning: Massachusetts had avoided the label “promissory estoppel” since Loranger but enforces promises by virtue of reliance under § 90; some decisions required a definite and certain promise, but Judge Young read § 90 and the Restatement’s definition of a promise in § 2 to require a commitment to act in a specified way, not a promise comprehensive enough to be an offer. Massachusetts cases had allowed reliance recovery where one party’s conduct kept the other on a string during negotiations, as in Pappas Industrial Parks and Greenstein. The Dixons fit that pattern: Wells Fargo told them that stopping payment and submitting information were the steps to a modification, must have expected them to comply, and its promise to consider them carried, as a matter of fair dealing, an undertaking not to foreclose on the very default it had produced; foreclosing without warning was “unseemly conduct at best.” To avoid chilling negotiations the remedy is limited to reliance: a footnote illustrated restoring the Dixons to their pre-default position by resuming payments with the arrears amortized over the loan, failing which Wells Fargo could foreclose.

cyberchron.summary: Where negotiations never produced a contract because essential terms stayed open, a buyer’s clear assurances that the supplier should keep producing and would be paid supported promissory estoppel for costs incurred after the promise; reliance damages may include reasonable overhead and shutdown costs but not expenses incurred before the promise or lost profits.

sections.Parties: Cyberchron Corporation, a manufacturer of rugged computer equipment, was the plaintiff. Calldata Systems Development, Inc., a subsidiary of Grumman Data Systems, was the defendant; the opinion calls the defendant’s side Grumman. Cyberchron sought payment for equipment it built; Calldata denied that any contract existed. Both sides appealed the judgment on Cyberchron’s promissory-estoppel claim.
sections.Material Facts: Grumman held a Marine Corps contract for the Advanced Tactical Air Command Central, and negotiated with Cyberchron to supply rugged components. The parties never agreed on the components’ weight or on penalties for exceeding weight limits; a May 15, 1990 purchase order specified a combined weight of 145 pounds and severe overweight penalties that Cyberchron never accepted. In July 1990 a Grumman representative told Cyberchron to proceed as if new weights had been approved and said the formal terms would be worked out later. In August Grumman’s director of material told Cyberchron it had a responsibility and obligation to keep performing to hold the schedule and indicated it could assume it would be paid. Meanwhile Grumman was negotiating with Codar Technology. On September 25, 1990 Calldata terminated the purchase order for default, and later bought heavier, inferior equipment from Codar. Between July 15 and September 25 Cyberchron spent $162,824.19 on labor and materials.
sections.Procedural History: Cyberchron sued in the Eastern District of New York. After a bench trial Judge Spatt held that no contract had formed because the parties never agreed on the essential weight and penalty terms, dismissed the contract and quantum meruit claims and Calldata’s counterclaim, and awarded Cyberchron $162,824.19 on promissory estoppel ($53,588.40 for materials and $109,235.79 for labor from July 15 to September 25, 1990), excluding overhead, lost profits and shutdown costs. Both parties appealed under New York law. The Second Circuit (Mahoney, J., with Walker and Sprouse, JJ.) affirmed liability, vacated the damages judgment and remanded on February 1, 1995, 47 F.3d 39.
sections.Issue: Where negotiations never produced a contract because essential terms remained unresolved, could the supplier recover under promissory estoppel for costs incurred after the buyer insisted that it continue performing? If so, what measure of reliance damages applies, and does it include overhead and shutdown costs?
sections.Holding: No contract existed because the parties never reached a meeting of the minds on essential terms, and that finding was not clearly erroneous. Under New York law promissory estoppel requires a clear and unambiguous promise, reasonable and foreseeable reliance, and injury sustained by reason of the reliance. Grumman’s July and August assurances and demands were such a promise, Cyberchron’s reliance was reasonable and foreseeable, and its injury was unconscionable, so injustice could be avoided only by enforcement. Recovery is limited to reliance damages, which include reasonable overhead where the claimant has a demonstrable history of ongoing operations and shutdown costs incurred because of the reliance. Liability affirmed; damages vacated and remanded.
sections.Reasoning: On estoppel the court applied the elements stated in Ripple’s of Clearview. The promise was clear: Grumman told Cyberchron to proceed as if the new weights were approved, refused to put that in writing but repeated it, and then insisted that Cyberchron was obligated to continue and could expect payment. Reliance was reasonable and foreseeable because Grumman was demanding exactly the performance Cyberchron undertook. Some New York decisions required an unconscionable injury, but the court treated Ripple’s as stating the rule and found the injury unconscionable in any event: Grumman pressed Cyberchron to produce at great expense while courting a competitor, then abruptly terminated and bought heavier, inferior equipment elsewhere. Only reliance after the clear promise was protected, so expenditures before July 15, when the parties were still negotiating without assurances, were not recoverable. Damages were reliance rather than lost profits, but the trial court erred in excluding overhead: it is an actual cost of doing business allocated by standard accounting, and a demonstrable history of ongoing operations suffices without proving that another project would have absorbed it.

channel-home.summary: An agreement to negotiate in good faith is an enforceable contract if it otherwise meets contract requirements; a landlord’s signed letter-of-intent promise to withdraw the store from the market and negotiate the lease only with the prospective tenant could bind him, and the tenant’s execution of the letter, which the landlord wanted to show lenders, was consideration.

sections.Parties: Channel Home Centers, a home-improvement retail chain operated as a division of Grace Retail Corporation, was the prospective tenant and plaintiff. Frank Grossman, a real-estate developer, and the entities through which he was acquiring a shopping mall were the defendants. Channel sought to enforce the letter of intent and stop Grossman from leasing the space to a competitor; Grossman maintained that the letter was a nonbinding preliminary document.
sections.Material Facts: Channel became interested in leasing space, and on December 11, 1984 sent Grossman a detailed letter of intent describing a 25-year lease of about 70,400 square feet with a rent schedule and percentage rent. It stated: “To induce the Tenant to proceed with the leasing of this Store, you will withdraw the Store from the rental market, and only negotiate the above described leasing transaction to completion.” Grossman had asked for such a letter to show “other people, banks or whatever,” and promptly signed and returned it. Both sides then worked toward a lease: Channel spent about $25,000 on measurements, plans, marketing and equipment; Grossman applied for zoning permits for Channel’s signs and exchanged draft leases. On February 6, 1985 Grossman ended negotiations, asserting a 30-day deadline the letter did not contain, and on February 7 leased the space to Mr. Good Buys at substantially higher rent.
sections.Procedural History: Channel sued in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania under diversity jurisdiction and sought a preliminary injunction. The district court consolidated the injunction hearing with trial on the merits under Rule 65(a)(2) without clear advance notice and held the letter unenforceable because it did not bind the parties, lacked consideration and failed Pennsylvania’s statute of frauds for leases; it also rejected Channel’s unilateral-contract and promissory-estoppel theories. The Third Circuit (Becker, J., with Weis and Higginbotham, JJ.) reversed and remanded on June 30, 1986, 795 F.2d 291, for trial on whether the parties intended to be bound and how long the duty to negotiate lasted.
sections.Issue: Under Pennsylvania law, is a landlord’s promise in a signed letter of intent to take the premises off the market and negotiate the lease only with the prospective tenant an enforceable contract even though the lease itself remained to be negotiated? Did the parties intend to be bound by that promise, was it supported by consideration, and was it sufficiently definite?
sections.Holding: An agreement to negotiate in good faith, if it otherwise meets the requirements of a contract, is enforceable. Under Pennsylvania law that turns on whether the parties manifested an intention to be bound, whether the terms are definite enough to enforce, and whether there was consideration. The evidence would support a finding that the parties intended to be bound by Grossman’s promise to withdraw the store from the market and negotiate exclusively with Channel; the promise was definite enough to enforce; and Channel’s execution and delivery of the letter, which Grossman wanted to obtain financing, was consideration. The statute of frauds was irrelevant because Channel did not claim the letter was a lease. Reversed and remanded.
sections.Reasoning: On intent the court looked to the whole letter and the surrounding circumstances. Most of the letter described lease terms the parties plainly expected to negotiate further, but the exclusive-negotiation clause was unequivocal, and the parties’ conduct afterward, Channel’s planning expenditures, Grossman’s zoning applications for Channel’s signs and the exchange of draft leases, was consistent with a binding commitment; that evidence supported, without compelling, a finding of intent to be bound. On definiteness the court distinguished an unenforceable agreement to agree on the lease itself from Grossman’s specific, discrete undertaking to take the property off the market and negotiate exclusively, whose breach a court could identify, and held with courts elsewhere that a good-faith negotiation agreement meeting contract requirements is enforceable. On consideration Grossman had requested the letter to show lenders, and Channel’s signature, backed by its corporate parent, strengthened his financing position, so Channel’s execution and tender of the letter was a bargained-for benefit. On remand the factfinder would decide intent and duration, including whether the claimed 30-day limit had been agreed and, if not, what period was reasonable.

sun-printing.summary: A contract leaving both the future price and the length of the period each price would govern to later agreement is an unenforceable agreement to agree as to those deliveries, even with a maximum price fixed by an external standard, because agreement on time was as essential as agreement on price and a court may not revise while professing to construe.

sections.Parties: Sun Printing and Publishing Association, a newspaper publisher, was the buyer of newsprint and the plaintiff. Remington Paper and Power Company, a newsprint manufacturer, was the seller and defendant. The buyer sought damages for the seller’s refusal to deliver paper during 1920; the seller maintained that its obligation for those months had never been fixed.
sections.Material Facts: In September 1919 the seller agreed to sell and the buyer to buy 1,000 tons of newsprint a month from September 1919 through December 1920. For the rest of the term it provided that “the price of the paper and length of terms for which such price shall apply shall be agreed upon by and between the parties hereto fifteen days prior to the expiration of each period for which the price and length of term thereof have been previously agreed upon,” the price “in no event to be higher than the contract price for newsprint charged by the Canadian Export Paper Company to the large consumers.” The seller delivered and was paid for the 1919 paper, then refused to agree on any 1920 price. The buyer demanded delivery at the Canadian Export price, and sued when the seller refused.
sections.Procedural History: The case was decided on the pleadings. Special Term ruled for the seller; the Appellate Division reversed and certified to the Court of Appeals the question whether the complaint stated a cause of action. On April 17, 1923 the Court of Appeals reversed the Appellate Division, affirmed Special Term’s judgment for the seller and answered the certified question in the negative, with costs. Judge Cardozo wrote for a five-judge majority (Hiscock, C.J., Pound, McLaughlin and Andrews, JJ.); Judge Crane dissented, joined by Judge Hogan.
sections.Issue: When a sales contract leaves the price and the period for which each price will apply to future agreement, subject to a maximum set by an external standard, is the seller bound to deliver at that maximum if the parties fail to agree, or is the provision an unenforceable agreement to agree?
sections.Holding: An agreement that leaves essential terms to future agreement is not enforceable as to those terms, and a court may not supply them by construction. Because the parties left open both the price and the length of the period during which each price would apply, and agreement on time was as essential as agreement on price, the 1920 provision was an agreement to agree; the seller was not bound to deliver at the Canadian price. The Court expressly did not decide whether the seller would have breached a duty by an arbitrary refusal to agree on a term after notice from the buyer, because the complaint did not rest on that theory.
sections.Reasoning: Cardozo agreed that the Canadian price was a maximum but held that the argument overlooked the second open term: the parties were to agree not only on a price but on the length of time it would apply, and once fixed it would stay fixed for that period even if the Canadian price moved. Agreement on a maximum payable this month is not agreement that it shall continue to be payable next month. Without an agreed period a court could not tell which Canadian price governed which deliveries, and if the buyer could invoke the Canadian price month by month it would hold not one option but a dozen, taking advantage of whatever price prevailed each month. The buyer’s fallback, that the seller had to accept a term reasonable in view of the trade’s practice, failed because the seller reserved the privilege of doing its business in its own way; to hold it to a standard of reasonableness would be to make the contract over, and courts are not at liberty to revise while professing to construe.

sun-printing.separateOpinions: Judge Crane, joined by Judge Hogan, dissented. The parties were business people who used a formal contract, drafted by the seller, to bind themselves to 16,000 tons of paper, and a court should presume they intended a binding agreement and give it effect if possible. A definite Canadian Export price existed on December 15, 1919, and if the buyer offered to pay that maximum the seller was bound to deliver; alternatively the court could apply the Canadian price in effect on the fifteenth of each month to that month’s thousand tons, or fix a reasonable period in light of trade practice.

oglebay.summary: When both pricing mechanisms of a long-term shipping contract failed, the parties’ decades of dealing showed they intended to remain bound, so the court could set a reasonable rate under the principles of Restatement § 33 and UCC § 2-305 and, because damages over the remaining term would be speculative, order the parties to negotiate and, failing that, mediate future rates.

sections.Parties: Oglebay Norton Company, which operated a fleet of Great Lakes bulk vessels, was the carrier and plaintiff, seeking a declaration that the contract remained in force and a determination of the rate. Armco, Inc., a steel producer, was the shipper and defendant, contending that the contract had become unenforceable because its pricing mechanisms had failed.
sections.Material Facts: Under a 1957 long-term contract Oglebay agreed to maintain vessel capacity to carry up to 7.1 million gross tons of Armco’s iron ore a year, and Armco agreed to use that capacity. Amendments extended the contract four times, ultimately through 2010; Oglebay undertook substantial capital investment, including a $95 million improvement program after the fourth amendment. The contract set the rate primarily by the rate recognized by leading iron-ore shippers, in practice the published rate for a leading shipper in Skillings Mining Review; failing that, the parties were to agree on a rate considering the rates of leading independent vessel operators. it failed: for 1985 the published rate was $7.41 per gross ton and Armco paid only $5.00, then the journal stopped publishing the rate and independent operators’ rates could not be obtained. The parties could not agree, and Armco took the position that the contract was no longer enforceable.
sections.Procedural History: Oglebay sought declaratory relief in the Court of Common Pleas, and in August 1987 Armco counterclaimed for a declaration that the contract was unenforceable. The trial court found that the parties intended to be bound despite the failure of the pricing mechanisms, set a reasonable rate of $6.25 per gross ton for the 1986 season on the parties’ course of dealing, their respective detriments and market comparisons reflecting the depressed steel industry, ordered them to negotiate a rate for each season through 2010 and to mediate if negotiations failed, and retained jurisdiction. The court of appeals affirmed, and the Supreme Court of Ohio affirmed per curiam on July 11, 1990, 52 Ohio St. 3d 232, all seven justices concurring.
sections.Issue: When both pricing mechanisms in a long-term contract fail, did the parties still intend to be bound? If so, may the court determine a reasonable price, and may it exercise continuing equitable jurisdiction by ordering the parties to negotiate future rates and, failing agreement, to mediate?
sections.Holding: Whether the parties intended to be bound despite the failure of their pricing mechanisms is a question of fact, and competent, credible evidence supported the finding that they did. When parties intend to conclude a contract but the price is not settled, a court may determine a reasonable price, as Restatement (Second) § 33 and its comments and UCC § 2-305(1), enacted in Ohio as R.C. 1302.18(A), recognize; the $6.25 rate fell within the range the evidence established. Because damages for breach of a contract of this length in a volatile market would be speculative, the trial court could order the equivalent of specific performance and require the parties to negotiate and, if necessary, mediate future rates. Affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: On intent the court deferred to the trial court’s finding, which rested on the parties’ long relationship, their course of dealing and the contract’s importance to both: Armco needed dedicated capacity, Oglebay had built and maintained its fleet to supply it, and nothing showed that the whole arrangement was meant to end if the published rate disappeared. On price the court relied on Restatement § 33, whose comment e recognizes that parties who intend to conclude a contract may leave the price unsettled and a court may then supply a reasonable price; UCC § 2-305(1) states the same principle for goods. Evidence that another steel producer paid $7.41 and another carrier quoted $5.90 for 1986 put $6.25 within a reasonable range. On remedy, Restatement § 362 permits specific performance when terms are certain enough to frame an order, using usage and terms supplied by law. Ordering negotiation and, if it broke down, mediation added nothing to the parties’ obligations; it supplied a practical means of carrying out a contract they had intended to last until 2010.
